[Series](index.qmd) · [Foundations](foundations.qmd) · [Violin](violin.qmd) · [Clarinet](clarinet.qmd) · [Kalimba](kalimba.qmd) · [Harmonica](harmonica.qmd) · **Piano** · [Drum](drum.qmd)
:::

A piano string is a violin string that is also a little bit of a kalimba tine. The two restoring forces add, and the overtones creep sharp.

::: {.family}
**Family: stiff strings.** Every real string is slightly stiff, so guitar and harp strings belong here too, faintly. The piano is where stiffness is large enough to hear, and large enough to shape how pianos are tuned.
:::

## Deriving the operator

A piano wire is under heavy tension, like a violin string, and it is thick steel, so it also resists bending, like a kalimba tine. Forces per unit length simply add: the tension term from the [foundations](foundations.qmd) and the bending term from the [kalimba](kalimba.qmd) give
$$
\mu\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx}, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \mathcal{L} = -c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4 .
$$

Treat the ends as pinned: they cannot move and transmit no bending moment, so $u = u_{xx} = 0$. Real piano strings are held closer to clamped, which shifts the numbers slightly but not the picture.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Step-by-step derivation</span>From Newton's law on a short piece of wire to the operator and its spectrum</summary>

**1. One small piece.** Follow the stretch of wire between $x$ and $x+dx$. Its mass is $\mu\,dx$ and its vertical acceleration is $u_{tt}$, so Newton's law says $\mu\,dx\,u_{tt}$ equals the net vertical force on it. Two forces act: the pull of tension, and the wire's resistance to bending.

**2. Tension.** The rest of the string pulls on each end of the piece with force $T$, along the string.

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 420 170" role="img" aria-label="A curved piece of string with tension pulling along the string at both ends">
  <path class="dash" d="M 20 130 L 400 130"/>
  <path class="acc" d="M 60 120 Q 210 40 360 120"/>
  <circle cx="110" cy="96" r="3" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="310" cy="96" r="3" class="fillacc"/>
  <path class="ink" d="M 110 96 L 52 127"/><path class="ink" d="M 310 96 L 368 127"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 110 96 L 110 140"/><path class="neg" d="M 310 96 L 310 140"/>
  <text x="34" y="122">T</text><text x="374" y="122">T</text>
  <text x="96" y="160">x</text><text x="292" y="160">x+dx</text>
  <text x="120" y="135">T u&#8339;(x)</text><text x="230" y="80">curved piece, mass &#956; dx</text>
  <text x="316" y="135">T u&#8339;(x+dx)</text>
</svg>
```

At the right end the pull points along the slope $u_x(x+dx)$, so for small slopes its vertical part is $T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta = T\,u_x(x+dx)$. At the left end it is $-T\,u_x(x)$. Together they give $T\,[u_x(x+dx) - u_x(x)] \approx T\,u_{xx}\,dx$. A curved piece feels a net pull toward its center of curvature; a straight piece feels none.

**3. Bending moment.** Bend the wire and its fibers no longer have equal lengths.

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 420 150" role="img" aria-label="A bent section of wire: fibers on the outside stretch, fibers on the inside compress, the middle keeps its length">
  <path class="bar" d="M 50 60 Q 210 10 370 60 L 370 100 Q 210 50 50 100 Z"/>
  <path class="dash" d="M 50 80 Q 210 30 370 80"/>
  <path class="pos" d="M 150 40 L 120 47"/><path class="pos" d="M 270 40 L 300 47"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 140 78 L 165 72"/><path class="neg" d="M 280 78 L 255 72"/>
  <text x="168" y="22">stretched (y &gt; 0)</text><text x="160" y="118">compressed (y &lt; 0)</text>
  <text x="300" y="138">neutral axis, y = 0</text>
</svg>
```

A fiber at height $y$ above the neutral axis is strained by $-y\,u_{xx}$, so by Hooke's law it carries the stress $\sigma = -E\,y\,u_{xx}$. These stresses cancel as forces but not as torques. Summed over the cross-section $A$, they give the bending moment
$$
M = -\int_A y\,\sigma\,dA = E\,u_{xx}\int_A y^2\,dA = EI\,u_{xx},
$$
where $I = \int_A y^2\,dA$ is the second moment of area. For a round wire of diameter $d$, $I = \pi d^4/64$.

**4. Shear.** Moments alone cannot move the piece up or down; vertical forces can. Each face of the piece also carries a vertical shear force.

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 420 170" role="img" aria-label="A thin slice with bending moments and shear forces on both faces">
  <path class="dash" d="M 30 85 L 390 85"/>
  <rect class="bar" x="150" y="65" width="120" height="40" rx="2"/>
  <path class="pos" d="M 136 55 A 32 32 0 0 0 136 115"/><path class="fillpos" d="M 130 113 L 140 120 L 141 109 Z"/>
  <path class="pos" d="M 284 55 A 32 32 0 0 1 284 115"/><path class="fillpos" d="M 290 113 L 280 120 L 279 109 Z"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 150 85 L 150 140"/><path class="fillneg" d="M 144 136 L 156 136 L 150 148 Z"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 270 85 L 270 30"/><path class="fillneg" d="M 264 34 L 276 34 L 270 22 Z"/>
  <text x="96" y="90">M</text><text x="306" y="90">M + dM</text>
  <text x="158" y="152">V</text><text x="278" y="30">V + dV</text><text x="198" y="128">dx</text>
</svg>
```

The piece is thin, so its rotational inertia is negligible and the torques on it must balance. Taking torques about the left face, the shear force on the right face times the lever arm $dx$ cancels the change in moment: $V\,dx + dM = 0$, so $V = -M_x$.

**5. Net bending force.** The two shear forces add up to $V(x+dx) - V(x) = V_x\,dx = -M_{xx}\,dx = -EI\,u_{xxxx}\,dx$.

**6. Newton's law.** Adding steps 2 and 5 gives $\mu\,dx\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx}\,dx - EI\,u_{xxxx}\,dx$. Dividing by $\mu\,dx$, with $c^2 = T/\mu$ and $\kappa^2 = EI/\mu$,
$$
u_{tt} = -\mathcal{L}u, \qquad \mathcal{L} = -c^2\partial_x^2 + \kappa^2\partial_x^4 .
$$

**7. Ends.** The bridge and the agraffe hold each end in place, so $u = 0$. If they let the wire pivot freely, they exert no moment, so $M = EI\,u_{xx} = 0$. These are the pinned conditions $u = u_{xx} = 0$.

**8. Spectrum.** Try $u = \sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)$ with $k = n\pi/L$, which satisfies both pinned conditions. Then $u_{xx} = -k^2u$ and $u_{xxxx} = k^4u$, so the equation becomes $-\omega^2 = -c^2k^2 - \kappa^2k^4$, that is
$$
\omega^2 = c^2k^2\Big(1 + \frac{EI}{T}\,k^2\Big) = \Big(\frac{n\pi c}{L}\Big)^2\Big(1 + \frac{\pi^2EI}{TL^2}\,n^2\Big).
$$
Taking square roots gives $f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}$, with $f_0 = c/2L$ and $B = \pi^2EI/TL^2$.

**9. How big is $B$?** For a middle C wire, roughly $d = 1$ mm, $L = 0.6$ m and $T = 700$ N, with steel's $E = 2\times10^{11}$ Pa: $I \approx 4.9\times10^{-14}$ m$^4$, so $B \approx 3.8\times10^{-4}$. The 10th partial then sits about 30 cents sharp. These numbers are rough; real strings vary.

**10. What was assumed.** Small slopes; tension unchanged as the wire flexes; the wire's rotational inertia neglected (Rayleigh's correction adds a small term); a uniform wire.

</details>
:::

## Spectrum

Pinned ends make $\sin(n\pi x/L)$ an eigenfunction of both terms at once. Substituting it gives $\omega^2 = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2 k^4$ with $k = n\pi/L$, so
$$
f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, \qquad B = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{T L^2}.
$$

The stiffness constant $B$ is small, but it multiplies $n^2$, so high partials run noticeably sharp. Since $I$ grows like the fourth power of the wire's diameter and $B$ falls like $1/L^2$, short thick treble strings are the stiffest.

## Hammer, dampers and pedals

The operator is only part of the string's equation. A real string is also pushed by the hammer and loses energy:
$$
\mu\,u_{tt} + b(x,t)\,u_t = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx} + f(x,t).
$$

Each term has one job. The operator, $T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx}$, fixes the frequencies and the mode shapes. The forcing $f$ is the hammer, and it fixes how much of each mode is excited. The damping $b$ is the felt dampers plus small internal losses, and it fixes how fast each mode dies. Every control a pianist touches acts on $f$ or on $b$. Only the tuner's wrench, which changes $T$, touches the operator.

Both effects are read off the mode shapes $X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L)$. A hammer blow at $x_h$ gives mode $n$ a weight proportional to $X_n(x_h)$, the same projection as for the [drum](drum.qmd). A damper felt resting on a short stretch $D$ of the string adds, to first order in $b$, the decay rate
$$
\gamma_n = \frac{\int_D b\,X_n^2\,dx}{2\mu\int_0^L X_n^2\,dx}.
$$
A mode is damped in proportion to how much it moves under the felt, and its frequency shifts only at second order. A mode with a node under the felt barely notices the damper: in the view below, slide the damper to $L/8$, where the hammer also sits, and the 8th mode is neither excited nor damped.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Step-by-step derivation</span>Where the hammer weights and the damping rates come from</summary>

**1. Expand in modes.** Write $u(x,t) = \sum_n q_n(t)\,X_n(x)$, with $\mathcal{L}X_n = \omega_n^2X_n$ and the pinned conditions.

**2. Project.** Substitute into the full equation, multiply by $X_m$ and integrate along the string. The operator is self-adjoint with these boundary conditions, so the $X_n$ are orthogonal: $\int_0^L X_mX_n\,dx = 0$ for $m \ne n$. The acceleration and operator terms collapse to one term each:
$$
\mu N_m\,(\ddot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m) + \sum_n B_{mn}\,\dot q_n = F_m(t),
$$
with $N_m = \int X_m^2\,dx$, $B_{mn} = \int b\,X_mX_n\,dx$ and $F_m = \int f\,X_m\,dx$.

**3. The hammer.** The felt touches a short stretch near $x_h$, so $F_m(t) \approx X_m(x_h)\,P(t)$, where $P(t)$ is the total force. Every mode gets the same push in time, weighted by $X_m(x_h)$: the mode's own height at the hammer.

**4. The damper.** If the damping is weak, the cross terms $B_{mn}$ with $m \ne n$ change the answer only at second order. Keeping the diagonal leaves a damped oscillator for each mode,
$$
\ddot q_m + 2\gamma_m\,\dot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m = 0, \qquad \gamma_m = \frac{B_{mm}}{2\mu N_m},
$$
whose solution $e^{-\gamma_m t}\cos\big(\sqrt{\omega_m^2 - \gamma_m^2}\,t\big)$ decays at the rate $\gamma_m$ while its frequency moves only by order $\gamma_m^2/\omega_m$.

**5. Honest limits.** A real damper is not weak: it stops a note in a fraction of a second. The formula gives the right picture, that modes are damped by how much they move under the felt, but not exact decay times.

</details>
:::

| Control | Term it changes | Effect |
|:--|:--|:--|
| key held down | $b$: lifts that note's damper | the note rings |
| key released | $b$: drops the damper on the string | mode $n$ decays at rate $\gamma_n$ |
| sustain pedal (right) | $b$: lifts every damper | released notes ring on |
| soft pedal (left) | $f$: the hammer strikes fewer strings (grand) or from closer (upright), with softer felt | quieter; high modes weaker |
| practice mute (middle, on uprights) | $f$: a felt strip sits between hammer and string | much quieter; most high modes gone |
| tuning pin | operator: the tension $T$ | every frequency moves |

On a grand piano the middle pedal is usually the *sostenuto*, which holds up only the dampers of keys already down. The soft pedal on a grand also changes how the two or three strings of a note share energy through the bridge, which reshapes the decay; this model leaves that out.

::: {.qa}
<details><summary><span class="label">Reader question</span>Why did the piano sound as if the sustain pedal were always down?</summary>

Because releasing a key did nothing. The first version let every string ring until it died on its own, and that is exactly what the sustain pedal does. On a real piano each key lifts a felt damper off its strings; letting go drops the damper back and stops the note within a fraction of a second. The sustain pedal lifts all the dampers at once, so released notes keep ringing. The keyboard above now models both. The top 20 keys have no dampers at all, as on a real piano: those short strings die out quickly by themselves.

</details>
:::

## Why tuners stretch octaves

A tuner sets an octave by listening for beats between the lower note's second partial and the upper note's fundamental. Stiffness pushes that second partial above $2f_0$, so a beat-free octave is slightly wider than 2 : 1. Repeated across the keyboard, this is *stretch tuning*: the top of a piano is tuned sharp of equal temperament, and the bottom flat.

    <p class="cap">Listen for the slow wobble in the 2 : 1 version. Raise the stiffness above to speed it up.</p>

(function () {

  var CODES = ["KeyA", "KeyW", "KeyS", "KeyE", "KeyD", "KeyF", "KeyT", "KeyG", "KeyY", "KeyH", "KeyU", "KeyJ", "KeyK", "KeyO", "KeyL", "KeyP", "Semicolon", "Quote"];

  var kbd = document.getElementById("kbd"), wrap = document.getElementById("kbdwrap"), btn = {}, wi = 0;
  for (var k = LOW; k <= HIGH; k++) if (!BLACK[k % 12]) wi++;
  kbd.style.width = (wi * WK) + "px";
  var x = 0;
  for (var k = LOW; k <= HIGH; k++) {
    var b = document.createElement("button"); b.type = "button"; b.dataset.key = k; b.tabIndex = -1;
    b.setAttribute("aria-label", C.noteName(C.mtof(k)).name);

  }

      b.textContent = inWin ? LABEL[i] : (k % 12 === 0 ? C.noteName(C.mtof(k)).name : "");
    }
    document.getElementById("winRead").innerHTML = "computer keys: <b>" + C.noteName(C.mtof(base)).name + "–" + C.noteName(C.mtof(base + CODES.length - 1)).name + "</b>";
    var el = btn[base]; if (el) wrap.scrollLeft = Math.max(0, parseFloat(el.style.left) - wrap.clientWidth / 2 + 4 * WK);
  }
  function shift(d) { base = Math.max(LOW + (12 - LOW % 12) % 12, Math.min(96, base + 12 * d)); labels(); }
  document.getElementById("octDown").addEventListener("click", function () { shift(-1); });

      var up = K.held || ped.sus, dz = damperZ(K);
      K.damper.position.set(K.x, ST_Y + 0.2 + (up ? 0.45 : 0), dz);
      railPos[3 * i] = K.x; railPos[3 * i + 1] = railY; railPos[3 * i + 2] = dz;
      var energy = 0;
      K.strings.forEach(function (line, j) {
        var pos = line.geometry.attributes.position.array, excited = !(ped.soft && j === 0), e = 0;
        for (var q = 0; q <= 48; q++) { var s = q / 48, y = excited ? shapeAt(K, s, t) * 0.45 : 0; pos[3 * q + 1] = ST_Y + y; e = Math.max(e, Math.abs(y)); }
        line.geometry.attributes.position.needsUpdate = true;
        line.material.color.setHex(e > 0.01 ? 0x2e4bb0 : 0x7d838e); energy = Math.max(energy, e);
      });

    });
    rail.geometry.attributes.position.needsUpdate = true;
    muteLabel.visible = ped.mute; railLabel.visible = ped.sus;
    tF.classList.toggle("on", forcing); tF.classList.toggle("mod", ped.soft || ped.mute);
    tD.classList.toggle("on", anyDamped && !ped.sus); tD.classList.toggle("off", ped.sus);
    controls.update(); renderer.render(scene, camera);
    drawWave(t); drawModes(t);
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(frame);
})();
</script>
